newsitem.title: JAPAN: Five Japan brokers probed over Taiwan payoffs.
newsitem.headline: Five Japan brokers probed over Taiwan payoffs.

text.p: Japanese commodity exchanges and government regulators are investigating possible payoffs to some favoured Taiwanese clients by five major commodity brokers, exchange officials told Reuters on Thursday.
An official at the Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM) said they were acting on information from Taiwan's Securities and Exchange Commission.
He said the suspected payoffs, apparently made in order to win Taiwanese business, seemed to come from the Taipei branches of the Japanese brokers.

The probe is another blow to Japan's financial world following news that linked top brokerage house Nomura Securities Co Ltd and foodstuffs maker Ajinomoto Co Inc with payoffs to corporate racketeers.
TOCOM held an emergency hearing on February 21 with heads of five Japanese commodity brokers currently operating in Taiwan, said Kazuhiko Senzaki, a director of TOCOM.
The five commodity brokers probed by TOCOM are Nihon Unicom Co, Tokyo General Co, Okato Shoji Co Ltd, Kobayashi Yoko Co Ltd and International Trading Co.
"At the hearing, we questioned them over whether they are making payoffs to Taiwanese clients," Senzaki told Reuters.
While an investigation is underway, authorities have not accused any of the firms of wrongdoing.
Other commodity brokers said one way brokers could unfairly compensate clients would be to grant them favourable prices on red bean contracts, which are actively traded in Japan.
Taiwanese orders to the Tokyo Grain Exchange (TGE) surged late last year, particularly for the often-volatile yen-based red bean futures contract, industry officials said.

Taiwan SEC futures department director Lo Ching-an, when contacted about the Tokyo investigation, confirmed that Japanese regulators had been in touch with his office but declined to say whether Taiwan officials had found any rules violations.
"They did visit us recently but we did not give any tips (about possible improprieties) to them," Lo told Reuters.
Lo said the SEC was conducting an investigation of Taiwan's futures and commodity brokerages, but called this routine.
"If we find that anyone has violated the rules, we will punish them," he said.
Officials contacted at the five brokers either said they believed their operations were sound, or declined to comment.
"We have operated (in Taiwan) in line with regulations, and will continue to do so," said Hirofumi Sugiyama, vice president of Nihon Unicom Co.
"In Taiwan we've been taking orders from investors carefully and think there's no wrongdoing," said Shigemitsu Hosogane of Kobayashi Yoko's International and Coporate department.
Japan's Ministry of Trade and Industry (MITI) was due to hold talks with TOCOM on Thursday about the suspected client compensation.
"We have not received an official notice from the Taiwanese SEC yet. But we may need to begin a probe into each broker if necessary," a MITI official said.
The TGE also said that it questioned the five commodity brokers over the suspected compensation on February 13, but did not disclose the details of the hearing.
Orders from Taiwan to the TGE during 1996 totalled 260,619 lots, the exchange said. Of those, red beans accounted for 107,938 lots, or 58.5 percent.
